Headline: City Council Approves New Greenway to Connect Downtown and Riverfront

Byline: By Maria Alvarez, City Desk

City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to approve a $12.5 million plan to develop a continuous greenway linking downtown to the riverfront, a move city officials say will boost local businesses and expand recreational opportunities for residents.

The project, which will convert an underused industrial corridor into a mix of pedestrian paths, bike lanes and native plantings, is scheduled to break ground this fall and open in phases over the next three years. Council members emphasized the project’s expected economic and public-health benefits during a packed public hearing in which neighborhood groups voiced both support and constructive concerns.

"This greenway will create safe, walkable connections between neighborhoods and bring new foot traffic to small businesses along Main Street," Mayor Elena Park said. "Investing in active transportation and public space is an investment in our community’s future."

Planners estimate the greenway will attract up to 250,000 visits annually once complete. Funding will come from a combination of municipal bonds, a state grant for urban revitalization, and a private donation from the Riverfront Foundation. The city also plans to pursue federal transportation grants to cover a portion of construction costs.

Some residents raised questions about parking availability and maintenance responsibilities. In response, the council directed the city’s parks department to prepare a maintenance plan and asked the planning staff to explore options for off-street parking and improved transit connections to minimize displacement of existing residents and businesses.

Construction will be phased to limit disruption to area businesses, with initial work focused on converting the corridor’s northern segment into a linear park and protected bike path. The parks department will host a series of community workshops this summer to gather input on planting palettes, lighting, and accessibility features.

Councilmember Jordan Lee, a longtime advocate for pedestrian infrastructure, said the greenway represents the culmination of years of community-driven planning. "This was shaped by residents and small-business owners who wanted a safe route for kids to walk and bike to school and for families to spend time outside," Lee said.

The city will hold its next public information session on June 4 at the community center. Officials encourage residents to attend and share their perspectives as design details are finalized.
